More Supermarket Botany

Modern citrus fruits contain numerous chemicals that affect human health and have a crazy evolutionary history. 

Citrus fruits (family, Rutaceae) are small trees or shrubs that include oranges, lemons, limes, and grapefruits. The fruit, a hesperidium, is a type of berry named after a Greek myth about nymphs (female nature deities) who were charged with caring for “golden apples” (probably oranges) in the Garden of Hesperides. It develops from a single flower with a superior compound ovary. The hesperidium, unlike a typical berry, has a tough outer rind or exocarp (also known as the flavedo), with numerous embedded oil glands. The white part of the rind is mesocarp (also known as the albedo), and the juicy edible parts of the fruit (the flesh) are made of ~8-16 segments that develop from the compound ovary of the flower. Each segment contains ovules that collectively yield a few up to 50 or more seeds in each fruit, although many popular citrus varieties are seedless. The fleshy segments contain swollen trichomes or juice vesicles that are surrounded by a membranous layer (endocarp). Citrus fruits as a group are considered non-climacteric, meaning they ripen on the tree and not after harvesting.

Citrus fruits contain a wide variety of phytochemicals. For example, numerous antioxidants, primarily flavonoids, are found in all parts of the fruit. Limonene is a terpene found primarily in the peel and is responsible, in part, for the odor associated with citrus fruits and many other plants. Citrus furanocoumarins, particularly bergapten, are chemicals that can cause phytophotodermatitis. This is a skin rash caused by the simultaneous exposure of skin to both UV light and citrus juice. Furanocoumarins (particularly in grapefruit) are also responsible for interactions with certain medications (e.g., statins, drugs to treat high blood pressure, certain antihistamines, and corticosteroids) because they interfere with enzymes that normally metabolize (breakdown) these drugs in the digestive system.

Wild ancestors of modern citrus fruits

The story of citrus fruits is complex. The center of diversity is certainly in the old world with ancient records obtained from India, China and elsewhere in southeast Asia showing the cultivation of wild citrus species. It does appear that four distinctive citrus ancestors have been hybridized and cultivated many times over the centuries, along with the asexual propagation of spontaneous mutations, to produce the citrus fruits found in our supermarket today. These ancestors are citron (C. medica), pummelo (C. maxima), mandarin orange (C. reticulata) and micrantha (C. hystix), some of which are still sold in the supermarket. 

Citron does not produce much juice; instead, the exocarp (flavedo) is utilized mostly for its pleasant fragrance and added to jams, sweets or to make wine and hard liquor. Very occasionally you will find a type of citron in the supermarket called “fingered citron” or Buddha’s Hand. Very fragrant and cool to see! The pummelo is typically easy to find amongst the produce as it is the biggest citrus fruit grown today, often weighing over two pounds. The pummelo is similar in appearance to a grapefruit, although it is a little sweeter in flavor, but with a very thick peel (mesocarp or albedo). Mandarin oranges are a small citrus variety with a sweet taste and a peel that is easy to separate from the juicy segments. A common variety of mandarin orange is the tangerine distinguished by having a slight reddish tinge to the flesh. (Plant breeders hybridized tangerines to both pummelos and grapefruit to produce distinct types of tangelos.) Both mandarin oranges and tangerines are eaten fresh, although mandarin oranges are typically sold as canned fruit. Micrantha citrus will not be available in the supermarket as the trees grow wild in the Philippines where the fruits are exploited for the oils extracted from the flavedo used locally as fragrances.
